source.module_title: Keil and Delitzsch Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Gen.4.1-Gen.4.8">Gen 4:1-8</reference> <div eID="gen100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101" type="x-p"/> The propagation of the human race did not commence till after the expulsion from paradise. Generation in man is an act of personal free-will, not a blind impulse of nature, and rests upon a moral self-determination. It flows from the divine institution of marriage, and is therefore knowing (ידע) the wife. - At the birth of the first son Eve exclaimed with joy, “<hi type="italic">I have gotten</hi> (קניתי) <hi type="italic">a man with Jehovah</hi>;” wherefore the child received the name <hi type="italic">Cain</hi> (קין from קוּן = קנה, κτᾶσθαι). So far as the grammar is concerned, the expression את־יהוה might be rendered, as in apposition to אישׁ, “<hi type="italic">a man, the Lord</hi>” (<hi type="italic">Luther</hi>), but the sense would not allow it. For even if we could suppose the faith of Eve in the promised conqueror of the serpent to have been sufficiently alive for this, the promise of God had not given her the slightest reason to expect that the promised seed would be of divine nature, and might be <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>, so as to lead her to believe that she had given birth to <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> now. את is a preposition in the sense of helpful association, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.21.20">Gen 21:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.39.2">Gen 39:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.39.21">Gen 39:21</reference>, etc. That she sees in the birth of this son the commencement of the fulfilment of the promise, and thankfully acknowledges the divine help in this display of mercy, is evident from the name <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>, the God of salvation. The use of this name is significant. Although it cannot be supposed that Eve herself knew and uttered this name, since it was not till a later period that it was made known to man, and it really belongs to the Hebrew, which was not formed till after the division of tongues, yet it expresses the feeling of Eve on receiving this proof of the gracious help of God.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Gen.4.9-Gen.4.10">Gen 4:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106" type="x-p"/> Defiance grows with sin, and punishment keeps pace with guilt. Adam and Eve fear before God, and acknowledge their sin; Cain boldly denies it, and in reply to the question, “<hi type="italic">Where is Abel thy brother?</hi>” declares, “<hi type="italic">I know not, am I my brother’s keeper?</hi>” God therefore charges him with his crime: “<hi type="italic">What hast thou done! voice of thy brother’s blood crying to Me from the earth</hi>.” The verb “<hi type="italic">crying</hi>” refers to the “<hi type="italic">blood</hi>,” since this is the principal word, and the <hi type="italic">voice</hi> merely expresses the adverbial idea of “aloud,” or “<hi type="italic">listen</hi>” (<hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §317 <hi type="italic">d</hi>). דּמים (drops of blood) is sometimes used to denote natural hemorrhage (<reference osisRef="Lev.12.4-Lev.12.5">Lev 12:4-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.20.18">Lev 20:18</reference>); but is chiefly applied to blood shed unnaturally, i.e., to murder. “Innocent blood has no voice, it may be, that is discernible by human ears, but it has one that reaches God, as the cry of a wicked deed demanding vengeance” (<hi type="italic">Delitzsch</hi>). Murder is one of the sins that cry to heaven. “<hi type="italic">Primum ostendit Deus se de factis hominum cognoscere utcunque nullus queratur vel accuset; deinde sibi magis charam esse homonum vitam quam ut sanguinem innoxium impune effundi sinat; tertio curam sibi piorum esse non solum quamdiu vivunt sed etiam post mortem</hi>” (Calvin). Abel was the first of the saints, whose blood is precious in the sight of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.15">Psa 116:15</reference>); and by virtue of his faith, he being dead yet speaketh through his blood which cried unto God (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.4">Heb 11:4</reference>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Gen.4.11-Gen.4.14">Gen 4:11-14</reference> <div eID="gen106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen107" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And now</hi> (sc., because thou hast done this) <hi type="italic">be cursed from the earth</hi>.” From: i.e., either away from the earth, driven forth so that it shall no longer afford a quiet resting-place (<hi type="italic">Gerlach</hi>, <hi type="italic">Delitzsch</hi>, etc.), or <hi type="italic">out of the earth</hi>, through its withdrawing its strength, and thus securing the fulfilment of perpetual wandering (<hi type="italic">Baumgarten</hi>, etc.). It is difficult to choose between the two; but the clause, “<hi type="italic">which hath opened her mouth</hi>,” etc. seems rather to favour the latter. Because the earth has been compelled to drink innocent blood, it rebels against the murderer, and when he tills it, withdraws its strength, so that the soil yields no produce; just as the land of Canaan is said to have spued out the Canaanites, on account of their abominations (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.28">Lev 18:28</reference>). In any case, the idea that “the soil, through drinking innocent blood, became an accomplice in the sin of murder,” has no biblical support, and is not confirmed by <reference osisRef="Isa.26.21">Isa 26:21</reference> or Num 35:33. The suffering of irrational creatures through the sin of man is very different from their participating in his sin. “<hi type="italic">A fugitive and vagabond</hi> (ונד נע, i.e., banished and homeless) <hi type="italic">shalt thou be in the earth</hi>.” Cain is so affected by this curse, that his obduracy is turned into despair, “<hi type="italic">My sin</hi>,” he says in <reference osisRef="Gen.4.13">Gen 4:13</reference>, “<hi type="italic">is greater than can be borne</hi>.” עון נשׁא signifies to take away and bear sin or guilt, and is used with reference both to God and man. God takes guilt away by forgiving it (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.7">Exo 34:7</reference>); man carries it away and bears it, by enduring its punishment (cf. Num 5:31). <hi type="italic">Luther</hi>, following the ancient versions, has adopted the first meaning; but the context sustains the second: for Cain afterwards complains, not of the greatness of the sin, but only of the severity of the punishment. “<hi type="italic">Behold, Thou hast driven me out this day from the face of the earth, and from Thy face shall I be hid;...and it shall come to pass that every one that findeth me shall slay me</hi>.” The <hi type="italic">adamah</hi>, from the face of which the curse of <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> had driven Cain, was Eden (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.4.16">Gen 4:16</reference>), where he had carried on his agricultural pursuits, and where God had revealed His face, i.e., His presence, to the men after their expulsion from the garden; so that henceforth Cain had to wander about upon the wide world, homeless and far from the presence of God, and was afraid lest any one who found him might slay him. By “<hi type="italic">every one that findeth me</hi>” we are not to understand <hi type="italic">omnis creatura</hi>, as though Cain had excited the hostility of all creatures, but every man; not in the sense, however, of such as existed apart from the family of Adam, but such as were aware of his crime, and knew him to be a murderer. For Cain is evidently afraid of revenge on the part of relatives of the slain, that is to say, of descendants of Adam, who were either already in existence, or yet to be born. Though Adam might not at this time have had “many grandsons and great-grandson,” yet according to <reference osisRef="Gen.4.17">Gen 4:17</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gen.5.4">Gen 5:4</reference>, he had undoubtedly other children, who might increase in number, and sooner or later might avenge Abel’s death. For, that blood shed demands blood in return, “is a principle of equity written in the heart of every man; and that Cain should see that earth full of avengers is just like a murderer, who sees avenging spirits (Ἐρινύες) ready to torture him on every hand.”

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Gen.4.15">Gen 4:15</reference> <div eID="gen107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen108" type="x-p"/> Although Cain expressed not penitence, but fear of punishment, God displayed His long-suffering and gave him the promise, “<hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> (לכן not in the sense of כן לא, but because it was the case, and there was reason for his complaint) <hi type="italic">whosoever slayeth Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold</hi>.” קין כּל־הרג, is <hi type="italic">cas</hi>. <hi type="italic">absolut</hi>. as in <reference osisRef="Gen.9.6">Gen 9:6</reference>; and הקּם avenged, i.e., resented, punished, as <reference osisRef="Exod.21.20">Exo 21:20</reference>-21. The mark which God put upon Cain is not to be regarded as a mark upon his body, as the Rabbins and others supposed, but as a certain sign which protected him from vengeance, though of what kind it is impossible to determine. God granted him continuance of life, not because banishment from the place of God’s presence was the greatest possible punishment, or because the preservation of the human race required at that time that the lives of individuals should be spared, - for God afterwards destroyed the whole human race, with the exception of one family, - but partly because the tares were to grow with the wheat, and sin develop itself to its utmost extent, partly also because from the very first God determined to take punishment into His own hands, and protect human life from the passion and wilfulness of human vengeance.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Gen.4.16-Gen.4.24">Gen 4:16-24</reference> <hi type="italic">The family of the Cainites</hi>. - Gen 4:16. The geographical situation of the land of <hi type="italic">Nod</hi>, in the front of Eden (קדמת, see <reference osisRef="Gen.2.14">Gen 2:14</reference>), where Cain settled after his departure from the place or the land of the revealed presence of God (cf. <reference osisRef="Jonah.1.3">Jon 1:3</reference>), cannot be determined. The name <hi type="italic">Nod</hi> denotes a land of flight and banishment, in contrast with Eden, the land of delight, where <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> walked with men. There Cain knew his wife. The text assumes it as self-evident that she accompanied him in his exile; also, that she was a daughter of Adam, and consequently a sister of Cain. The marriage of brothers and sisters was inevitable in the case of the children of the first men, if the human race was actually to descend from a single pair, and may therefore be justified in the face of the Mosaic prohibition of such marriages, on the ground that the sons and daughters of Adam represented not merely the family but the genus, and that it was not till after the rise of several families that the bands of fraternal and conjugal love became distinct from one another, and assumed fixed and mutually exclusive forms, the violation of which is sin. (Comp. Lev 18.) His son he named <hi type="italic">Hanoch</hi> (consecration), because he regarded his birth as a pledge of the renovation of his life. For this reason he also gave the same name to the city which he built, inasmuch as its erection was another phase in the development of his family. The construction of a city by Cain will cease to surprise us, if we consider that at the commencement of its erection, centuries had already passed since the creation of man, and Cain’s descendants may by this time have increased considerably in numbers; also, that עיר does not necessarily presuppose a large town, but simply an enclosed space with fortified dwellings, in contradistinction to the isolated tents of shepherds; and lastly, that the words בנה ויהי, “he was building,” merely indicate the commencement and progress of the building, but not its termination. It appears more surprising that Cain, who was to be a fugitive and a vagabond upon the earth, should have established himself in the land of Nod. This cannot be fully explained, either on the ground that he carried on the pursuits of agriculture, which lead to settled abodes, or that he strove against the curse. In addition to both the facts referred to, there is also the circumstance, that the curse, “the ground shall not yield to thee her strength,” was so mollified by the grace of God, that Cain and his descendants were enabled to obtain sufficient food in the land of his settlement, though it was by dint of hard work and strenuous effort; unless, indeed, we follow <hi type="italic">Luther</hi> and understand the curse, that he should be a fugitive upon the earth, as relating to his expulsion from Eden, and his removal <hi type="italic">ad incertum locum et opus, non addita ulla vel promissione vel mandato, sicut avis quae in libero caelo incerta vagatur</hi>. The fact that Cain undertook the erection of a city, is also significant. Even if we do not regard this city as “the first foundation-stone of the kingdom of the world, in which the spirit of the beast bears sway,” we cannot fail to detect the desire to neutralize the curse of banishment, and create for his family a point of unity, as a compensation for the loss of unity in fellowship with God, as well as the inclination of the family of Cain for that which was earthly. <div eID="gen108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen109" type="x-p"/> The powerful development of the worldly mind and of ungodliness among the Cainites was openly displayed in Lamech, in the sixth generation. Of the intermediate links, the names only are given. (On the use of the passive with the accusative of the object in the clause “<hi type="italic">to Hanoch was born</hi> (they bore) <hi type="italic">Irad</hi>,” see <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> §143, 1.) Some of these names resemble those of the Sethite genealogy, viz., Irad and Jared, Mehujael and Mahalaleel, Methusael and Methuselah, also Cain and Cainan; and the names Enoch and Lamech occur in both families. But neither the recurrence of similar names, nor even of the same names, warrants the conclusion that the two genealogical tables are simply different forms of one primary legend. For the names, though similar in sound, are very different in meaning. <hi type="italic">Irad</hi> probably signifies the townsman, <hi type="italic">Jared</hi>, descent, or that which has descended; <hi type="italic">Mehujael</hi>, smitten of God, and <hi type="italic">Mahalaleel</hi>, praise of God; <hi type="italic">Methusael</hi>, man of prayer, and Methuselah, man of the sword or of increase.
